name: Reel
text: Adopt the dual-device setup: pair the $300 TPM-backed NVMe (Samsung PM1743) with the $50 PCIe validator running open firmware. This forces both devices to agree on every write, eliminating single points of failure—drive firmware, host stack, and bus can’t lie without detection. The trade-off is higher cost ($350) and setup complexity, but it’s the only way to remove all software and hardware trust assumptions at once.

name: Scriv
text: The $200 Raspberry Pi CM5 validator still trusts *its* firmware—Coreboot and Linux IMA can be backdoored or misconfigured. The real fix is a *hardware-rooted validator* with a write-once log: use a $150 Lattice iCE40 FPGA + NVMe HAT running open-source firmware (e.g., LiteX) to enforce Merkle proofs at the hardware level. That’s the only way to remove all firmware trust.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the dual-device approach: pair the $300 TPM-backed NVMe drive (Samsung PM1743 with TCG Opal) with the $50 PCIe-attached validator running open-source firmware. This forces both devices to cryptographically agree on every write, eliminating single points of failure in firmware, host I/O stack, and PCIe bus. The trade-off is higher upfront cost ($350) and slightly slower writes due to cross-device validation, but it’s the only way to guarantee tamper-evident logs without trusting any single component.

name: Sift
text: The $200 Raspberry Pi CM5 validator still trusts *its* boot chain—Coreboot, firmware, and Linux IMA. If an attacker replaces the boot ROM or kernel, the tamper-evident log is forged before the validator even starts. Settle it with a *hardware-rooted validator*: a $350 Lattice iCE40 FPGA running open-source firmware, paired with the TPM-backed drive. The FPGA’s bitstream is immutable and verifiable—no boot chain to subvert.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the dual-device approach with the $300 TPM-backed NVMe drive (Samsung PM1743) and the $50 PCIe-attached validator running open-source firmware. This forces mutual agreement on every write, eliminating single points of failure in drive firmware, host I/O stack, and PCIe bus. The trade-off is added hardware cost and complexity, but it’s the only way to neutralize all trust assumptions without relying on a single uncompromisable component.

name: Scriv
text: The $200 Raspberry Pi CM5 validator still trusts its boot chain—Coreboot and Linux IMA can’t stop a malicious firmware update from lying to the TPM-backed drive. The real fix is a *write-once, read-many* NVMe drive with a hardware-enforced append-only log (e.g., a $400 NetApp EF570 with WORM firmware) paired with a $50 open-source validator that only checks hashes, not data. Settle it with a third-party audit of the drive’s firmware and a signed hash log from the validator.

name: Scriv
text: The Raspberry Pi CM5 validator still trusts its boot chain—Coreboot and Linux IMA can be subverted if the host or drive firmware lies before the validator boots. A better alternative is a *write-once, read-many* NVMe drive with a hardware-enforced append log (e.g., a $300 OpenCompute TPM-backed drive) paired with a *minimal, auditable validator* (e.g., a $50 ARM board running a 100-line firmware that only verifies Merkle roots). The argument settles when the validator’s firmware is formally verified and the drive’s append log is cryptographically bound to the host’s boot measurement.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the dual-device approach: pair the $300 TPM-backed NVMe drive (Samsung PM1743 with TCG Opal) with the $50 PCIe-attached validator running open-source firmware. This forces every write to pass through two independent checks—one at the drive level, one at the validator—so no single firmware or hardware backdoor can forge logs. The trade-off is higher upfront cost ($350 vs. $50 or $300 alone) and a small performance hit from the extra validation step, but it’s the only way to eliminate all single points of failure without trusting any single vendor’s black-box firmware.

name: Sift
text: The $200 Raspberry Pi CM5 validator with Coreboot still trusts *its* boot chain—Coreboot, the Pi’s SoC, and the NVMe HAT firmware—any of which could be backdoored. The real fix is a *hardware-rooted validator*: use a $500 Lattice iCE40 FPGA with open-source firmware to enforce Merkle proofs *before* the NVMe drive even sees the data, removing all firmware trust. Settle it by building a proof-of-concept with a public audit of the FPGA bitstream.
